query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 FCC high‐entropy alloy, degradation at elevated temperatures in oxidizing versus reducing atmospheres is governed by element‐selective oxidation at grain boundaries. In oxidizing gases, preferential oxidation of the minor Al and Ti leads to the development of a discontinuous, stress‐inducing oxide network along grain boundaries that eventually triggers catastrophic failure. In contrast, reducing conditions inhibit extensive oxide formation and thereby slow degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated alloy exhibiting a uniform FCC matrix with fine microstructure, minimal segregation, and an initially intact surface oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Controlled change of gas atmosphere during high-temperature exposure: comparing oxidizing conditions (oxygen-containing environment) versus reducing conditions (hydrogen-rich or inert gas environment).
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (e.g., 800–1000 °C) for prolonged exposures (e.g., 10 hours or more) with careful control of gas composition.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and evolution of a grain boundary and sub-grain oxide network (enriched in Al and Ti) that induces internal stresses and crack initiation.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, the preferential oxidation of trace Al and Ti creates discontinuous oxide patches at the grain boundaries. These patches coalesce into a network that, due to mismatch in thermal expansion and growth stresses, introduces micro-cracks that propagate and lead to eventual catastrophic failure. Under reducing conditions, the inhibited oxide formation prevents or delays such grain boundary deterioration.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing exposure, microstructural analysis will reveal extensive grain boundary oxidation, increased oxide scale thickness, and evidence of crack nucleation; mechanical testing should show a significant drop in strength and ductility relative to the baseline. Under reducing conditions, these deleterious changes will be substantially reduced or absent, maintaining baseline mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated state with a uniform FCC microstructure showing minimal pre-existing oxidation and high mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to elevated-temperature exposures (approx. 800–1000 °C) and over time intervals where diffusion-controlled oxidation is significant; behavior outside these boundaries (e.g., lower temperatures or very short exposure times) may not follow the same mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of the oxide network formation and the quantitative contribution of each element (Al vs. Ti) to the degradation process remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the alloy in identical form and expose them at 900 °C for 10 hours in two atmospheres – one oxidizing (e.g., air or oxygen-enriched) and one reducing (e.g., hydrogen or inert gas environment). Post-exposure, perform detailed microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM and EDS mapping) focusing on grain boundaries, and conduct mechanical tests (tensile strength, fracture toughness).
measurements: Thickness and continuity of oxide layers at grain boundaries via SEM/TEM imaging.
Elemental distribution of Al and Ti at grain boundaries using EDS or atom probe tomography.
Mechanical property changes (strength, ductility, fracture toughness) relative to the as-fabricated baseline.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidizing condition does not produce significantly increased grain boundary oxidation (in terms of oxide continuity, thickness, and stress-induced cracking) relative to the reducing condition, or if the mechanical degradation under oxidizing conditions is not significantly worse than that under reducing conditions, then the hypothesis that selective grain boundary oxidation governs failure is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractIn the present study, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was fabricated by laser melting deposition (LMD). Then, post-heat treatment was performed at different temperatures to investigate its effects on microstructure and corrosion property of the alloy. The results obtained from microstructural characterization indicate that the alloy, whether heat-treated or not, exhibited a lamellar eutectic microstructure composed of alternating FCC and BCC phases. With the increase in the heating temperature from 600 to 1000 °C, the interlamellar spacing and volume fraction of the FCC phase gradually increased. Electrochemical testing in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution revealed that the resistance of the alloy to corrosion was improved with the increasing heating temperature, which was attributed to the increased volume fraction of the FCC phase. However, the immersion test in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution also suggests that heating above 800 °C increased the susceptibility of the alloy to pitting corrosion, due to the more pronounced enrichment of Al in the BCC phase.Keywords: additive manufacturing, eutectic high-entropy alloy, heat treatment, microstructure, corrosion resi
